stem: The chapter 'Alternative Centres of Power' discusses the rise of new power centres that could balance US dominance. Two of the most important such centres it focuses on are __________.
options: The European Union (EU) and the ASEAN/China (in Asia)
The USSR and the Warsaw Pact
NATO and CENTO
The League of Nations and the UN
solution: The chapter 'Alternative Centres of Power' examines the emergence of new centres of power in world politics that could serve as alternatives to, and potential balancers of, US dominance. It focuses especially on the EUROPEAN UNION (EU) in Europe, and on ASEAN and the rise of CHINA in Asia (along with the broader growth of Asian economies). These represent regional and national power centres challenging the unipolar order. So the two main centres discussed are the EU and ASEAN/China. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The European Union (EU) evolved from earlier efforts at European economic cooperation after the Second World War. A key early step was the __________.
options: Formation of the European Economic Community (EEC) / European Community, building on cooperation like the European Coal and Steel Community
Creation of NATO
Signing of the Warsaw Pact
Founding of ASEAN
solution: The European Union evolved through stages of European economic (and later political) integration after the Second World War. Key early steps included the European Coal and Steel Community and then the formation of the European Economic Community (EEC) / European Community — cooperative bodies that progressively integrated the economies of Western European states. Over time this deepened into the European Union (established by the Maastricht Treaty in 1992). So a key early step was the EEC/European Community. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The European Union was formally established by the __________ in 1992.
options: Maastricht Treaty
Treaty of Versailles
Warsaw Treaty
Treaty of Tordesillas
solution: The European Union (EU) was formally established by the MAASTRICHT TREATY (the Treaty on European Union) in 1992. This treaty deepened European integration — creating the EU, laying the basis for a common currency (the euro) and common foreign, security, and justice policies, and moving Europe beyond a purely economic community toward a closer political and economic union. So the EU was established by the Maastricht Treaty (1992). This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The common currency adopted by many EU member states is the __________.
options: Euro
Dollar
Pound
Franc
solution: The common currency adopted by many (though not all) EU member states — those forming the 'eurozone' — is the EURO. Its introduction created a single currency shared across a large economic bloc, deepening economic integration and giving the EU a currency that can rival the US dollar in international finance and trade. So the EU's common currency is the euro. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The EU is described as an influential power because its combined strength spans several dimensions. Which of the following is one such source of EU influence?
options: Its huge combined economy (one of the largest in the world) and its role as a major trading power and aid/donor
Only its military might
Only its population
Only its tourism
solution: The EU is an influential power partly because of its combined ECONOMIC strength: taken together, its member states form one of the LARGEST ECONOMIES in the world, and the EU is a major global TRADING power (its share of world trade is very large) and a leading source of economic AID and investment (donor). This economic weight gives the EU significant leverage and influence in international economic and political affairs. So one source of EU influence is its huge combined economy and trade/aid role. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The EU also exercises influence through political and diplomatic means. Which of the following reflects this?
options: Two of its members (France and, formerly, the UK) hold permanent seats on the UN Security Council, and the EU plays an active diplomatic role in world affairs
It has no diplomatic influence at all
It controls the UN entirely
It has no members in any international body
solution: The EU exercises significant political and DIPLOMATIC influence. Notably, two of its members — FRANCE and (before Brexit) the United Kingdom — hold PERMANENT SEATS (with veto power) on the UN SECURITY COUNCIL, and several EU members are influential states in their own right. The EU also plays an active collective DIPLOMATIC role in world affairs (negotiating on trade, climate, and various global issues, and using diplomacy and economic leverage rather than force). So EU political influence is reflected in its UN Security Council seats and active diplomacy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A limitation on the EU's ability to act as a unified power is that __________.
options: Its member states retain their own sovereignty, national interests, and foreign/defence policies, so they do not always agree or act together on major issues
It has no economy
It has too few members
Its members always agree on everything
solution: A key LIMITATION on the EU acting as a fully unified power is that its member states remain SOVEREIGN nations, each with its own NATIONAL INTERESTS and its own FOREIGN and DEFENCE policies. On many major international issues, the members do NOT always AGREE or act TOGETHER (there are internal differences and reluctance to cede sovereignty in sensitive areas like foreign policy and defence). This lack of a single, unified will limits the EU's ability to project power as coherently as a single state. So the limitation is that member states retain sovereignty and often differ. So option 1 is correct.

stem: ASEAN stands for the __________.
options: Association of Southeast Asian Nations
Alliance of Soviet and European Nations
Asian Security and Economic Network
African Society of Eastern Nations
solution: ASEAN stands for the ASSOCIATION of SOUTHEAST ASIAN NATIONS. It is a regional organisation of Southeast Asian countries, formed to promote economic cooperation, peace, stability, and mutual development in the region. It has become an important alternative centre of power and a model of regional cooperation in Asia. So ASEAN = Association of Southeast Asian Nations. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: ASEAN was established in 1967 by the __________ (Bangkok Declaration).
options: Founding members Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand
USA and USSR
China and Japan
India and Pakistan
solution: ASEAN was established in 1967 through the Bangkok Declaration by its five FOUNDING members: INDONESIA, MALAYSIA, the PHILIPPINES, SINGAPORE, and THAILAND. Over the following decades its membership expanded to include other Southeast Asian countries (like Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, and Cambodia), growing into a ten-member regional grouping. So ASEAN was founded in 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The main objectives behind the formation of ASEAN were to __________.
options: Accelerate economic growth, promote regional peace and stability, and foster social/cultural cooperation among member states
Build a nuclear arsenal
Conquer neighbouring regions
Join a Cold War military bloc
solution: The main OBJECTIVES behind the formation of ASEAN were to: ACCELERATE ECONOMIC GROWTH and development through regional cooperation; promote regional PEACE and STABILITY (based on respect for the rule of law and the principles of the UN Charter, and non-interference in each other's affairs); and foster SOCIAL and CULTURAL cooperation and collaboration among the member states. ASEAN emphasised cooperation, dialogue, and consensus (the 'ASEAN Way') rather than confrontation. So its objectives were economic growth, peace/stability, and social-cultural cooperation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The relaxed, consensus-based, non-confrontational style of interaction and decision-making that characterises ASEAN is often called the __________.
options: 'ASEAN Way'
'Cold War Way'
'Warsaw method'
'Marshall style'
solution: The distinctive style of interaction and decision-making that characterises ASEAN is often called the 'ASEAN WAY'. It emphasises a RELAXED, informal, CONSENSUS-based, and NON-CONFRONTATIONAL approach — resolving matters through dialogue, quiet diplomacy, mutual respect, non-interference in members' internal affairs, and consensus rather than through binding rules, majority voting, or confrontation. This cooperative style has helped diverse Southeast Asian states work together peacefully. So the ASEAN style is called the 'ASEAN Way'. This is a prelims-relevant term.

stem: ASEAN has moved toward closer economic integration, aiming to create the __________.
options: ASEAN Economic Community (and a Free Trade Area/AFTA)
European Union
Warsaw Pact economy
A single ASEAN nuclear force
solution: ASEAN has increasingly moved toward closer ECONOMIC INTEGRATION. It established the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) to reduce trade barriers among members, and it has worked toward creating an ASEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY (AEC) — aiming for a more integrated single market and production base, with freer flows of goods, services, investment, and skilled labour among member states. This deepening economic cooperation strengthens ASEAN as an economic power centre. So ASEAN aims at an ASEAN Economic Community (and AFTA). So option 1 is correct.

stem: China's dramatic rise as an economic power began especially with the economic reforms initiated in __________.
options: 1978, under Deng Xiaoping (the 'open door' policy and market reforms)
1949, under Mao Zedong
2001, under the WTO only
1911, under the last emperor
solution: China's dramatic rise as an economic power began especially with the ECONOMIC REFORMS initiated in 1978 under the leadership of DENG XIAOPING. These reforms opened up the Chinese economy (the 'open door' policy) and gradually introduced MARKET mechanisms, private enterprise, and foreign investment — while retaining Communist Party political control. This transformation set off decades of rapid, sustained economic growth that turned China into a major global power. So China's reforms began in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: China's economic model since 1978 is often described as __________.
options: A 'socialist market economy' — retaining Communist Party political control while introducing market reforms and opening to global trade and investment
A fully free-market democracy
A pure Soviet-style command economy unchanged
A subsistence agrarian economy with no industry
solution: China's economic model since 1978 is often described as a 'SOCIALIST MARKET ECONOMY'. It combines the RETENTION of COMMUNIST PARTY political control (a one-party state) with the INTRODUCTION of MARKET reforms — allowing private enterprise, special economic zones, foreign investment, and integration into global TRADE — while the state still plays a major guiding role in the economy. This distinctive blend of authoritarian politics and market-oriented economics fuelled China's rapid growth. So China's model is a 'socialist market economy'. So option 1 is correct.

stem: China's rise is significant for world politics because __________.
options: Its rapid economic growth has made it the world's second-largest economy and a rising military and political power, giving it growing influence and making it a potential rival/balancer to the USA
It has become smaller and weaker
It has no effect on world affairs
It joined NATO
solution: China's rise is highly significant for world politics because its rapid, sustained ECONOMIC GROWTH has made it the world's SECOND-LARGEST ECONOMY, a manufacturing and trading giant, and an increasingly powerful MILITARY and POLITICAL actor. This growing wealth and power give China expanding INFLUENCE across the world (through trade, investment, diplomacy, and institutions), and make it the most significant potential RIVAL to, and BALANCER of, US dominance — a key driver of the shift toward a more multipolar world. So China's rise makes it a rising power and potential balancer to the USA. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's relations with China are complex, involving both cooperation and tensions. A key area of tension is __________.
options: The unresolved border/boundary dispute (which led to a war in 1962) and strategic rivalry, even as trade and economic ties have grown
A shared currency
A joint military alliance against all others
The lack of any border between them
solution: India–China relations are complex, mixing COOPERATION and TENSION. A key area of TENSION is the long-unresolved BORDER/boundary DISPUTE (over which the two fought a war in 1962) and their broader STRATEGIC RIVALRY (including competition for influence in Asia, China's ties with Pakistan, and issues like Tibet and trade imbalances). At the same time, ECONOMIC and TRADE ties between the two have grown substantially, and they cooperate on some global issues (e.g., in forums like BRICS and on climate/trade). So a key tension is the border dispute and strategic rivalry, alongside growing trade. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rise of alternative centres of power (like the EU, ASEAN, and China) is significant for the international order because it __________.
options: Points toward a more multipolar world, in which power is distributed among several centres rather than concentrated in a single hegemon
Guarantees permanent US dominance
Means the return of a bipolar Cold War
Has no effect on the distribution of power
solution: The rise of alternative centres of power — such as the EU, ASEAN, and especially China (and others like India, Japan, and Russia) — is significant because it points toward a more MULTIPOLAR world: an international order in which POWER and influence are DISTRIBUTED among SEVERAL major centres, rather than being concentrated in a SINGLE dominant hegemon (the USA). As these centres grow in economic and political weight, they can increasingly balance, check, and share global influence, transforming the unipolar post-Cold-War order. So the rise of alternative centres points toward multipolarity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The success of ASEAN and the EU as regional organisations demonstrates the value of __________.
options: Regional cooperation and integration — pooling strengths, resolving disputes peacefully, and boosting economic development and collective influence
Constant warfare between neighbours
Complete isolation of each country
Abolishing all national governments
solution: The success of ASEAN and the EU as regional organisations demonstrates the VALUE of REGIONAL COOPERATION and INTEGRATION. By POOLING their strengths (economic, political, diplomatic), member states can: boost ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT and prosperity (through larger markets, trade, and investment); resolve disputes PEACEFULLY and maintain regional stability; and amplify their COLLECTIVE INFLUENCE on the world stage (far greater than any one member alone). These regional bodies thus become significant power centres and models of cooperation. So they demonstrate the value of regional cooperation and integration. So option 1 is correct.

stem: China's growing economic ties with countries around the world (trade, investment, loans, and infrastructure projects) give it __________.
options: Considerable political influence and leverage in many regions (economic power translating into strategic/diplomatic influence)
No influence at all
A weaker global position
Only cultural influence
solution: China's growing ECONOMIC TIES with countries across the world — through TRADE, INVESTMENT, LOANS, and large INFRASTRUCTURE projects (such as ports, roads, and railways, notably under initiatives like the Belt and Road) — give it considerable POLITICAL INFLUENCE and LEVERAGE in many regions (in Asia, Africa, Latin America, and beyond). As countries become economically linked to and dependent on China, its economic power TRANSLATES into strategic and DIPLOMATIC influence, extending its reach as a rising global power. So China's economic ties give it considerable political influence. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The EU is a powerful actor but not a unified state. Reason (R): While the EU has a common market, currency (for many), and combined economic clout, its member states retain sovereignty over key areas like foreign and defence policy and often differ. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the EU is a powerful actor but NOT a single unified state. And the reason is (R) that, while the EU has achieved deep integration in some areas (a common market, a shared currency for many members, and enormous combined economic clout), its member states RETAIN SOVEREIGNTY over KEY areas — especially FOREIGN and DEFENCE policy — and they often DIFFER and pursue their own national interests on major issues. This retention of national sovereignty and the resulting internal differences are precisely why the EU cannot act as a fully unified state (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): China chose to introduce market reforms while keeping the Communist Party's political monopoly. Reason (R): This 'gradual', state-guided opening (rather than 'shock therapy') allowed China to achieve rapid growth while maintaining political control and stability. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that China introduced MARKET reforms while KEEPING the Communist Party's POLITICAL MONOPOLY (economic opening without political liberalisation). And the reason is (R) that this GRADUAL, STATE-GUIDED, and phased opening — in contrast to the abrupt 'SHOCK THERAPY' of the former Soviet states — allowed China to achieve RAPID economic GROWTH while MAINTAINING firm political CONTROL and STABILITY (avoiding the economic collapse and disorder that afflicted post-Soviet transitions). This approach explains why China combined reform with party control (A). So R correctly explains A. This contrast with shock therapy is an important point.

stem: India's approach to the rise of these alternative centres of power (EU, ASEAN, China) has been to __________.
options: Engage and strengthen ties with them (e.g., 'Look East'/'Act East' policy toward ASEAN, and economic ties with the EU and China) as part of building a multipolar world and advancing its interests
Isolate itself from all of them
Declare war on all of them
Ignore them completely
solution: India's approach to the rise of alternative centres of power has been to ENGAGE with and STRENGTHEN TIES with them, as part of building a more multipolar world and advancing its own interests. For example, India has pursued a 'LOOK EAST' (later 'ACT EAST') policy to deepen economic and strategic ties with ASEAN and East Asia; it has developed substantial economic and trade relations with the EU; and it manages a complex relationship of engagement (especially economic) with CHINA, even amid rivalry. India also participates in groupings (like BRICS) that bring together emerging powers. So India engages with these centres to advance its interests and a multipolar order. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter's broader point about 'alternative centres of power' is that __________.
options: The world is gradually moving away from unchallenged US unipolarity toward a system with multiple significant power centres, shaped by economic growth and regional cooperation
US dominance will never be challenged
Only military power creates influence
Regional organisations always fail
solution: The broader point of the chapter on 'alternative centres of power' is that the world is GRADUALLY MOVING AWAY from unchallenged US unipolarity toward a system with MULTIPLE significant POWER CENTRES (a more multipolar order). This shift is being driven largely by ECONOMIC GROWTH (the rise of economies like China and India) and by successful REGIONAL COOPERATION and integration (as with the EU and ASEAN), which are building up new poles of economic and political influence capable of balancing and complementing US power. So the chapter's point is the gradual emergence of a more multipolar world through economic growth and regional cooperation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches the alternative power centre with a key feature?
options: EU — deep economic/political integration and a common currency (euro); ASEAN — regional cooperation via the 'ASEAN Way' and economic integration; China — rapid growth via a 'socialist market economy'
EU — a military dictatorship; ASEAN — a single nation; China — a free-market democracy
EU — no economy; ASEAN — a Cold War bloc; China — an agrarian state
All three are identical
solution: The correct matching is: the EU — characterised by DEEP economic and political INTEGRATION and a COMMON CURRENCY (the euro for many members); ASEAN — characterised by regional COOPERATION conducted through the consensual 'ASEAN WAY' and moving toward ECONOMIC integration (AFTA/AEC); and CHINA — characterised by RAPID economic GROWTH achieved through its reform-era 'SOCIALIST MARKET ECONOMY' (market reforms under continued Communist Party rule). So option 1 correctly pairs each centre with its key feature. This is a useful summary for prelims.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Alternative Centres of Power' is that:
options: The USA will forever remain the only power centre

As the post-Cold-War unipolar world evolves, new alternative centres of power have emerged to balance and complement US dominance — notably the European Union (a deeply integrated economic and political bloc with the euro and major global clout, though limited by its members' retained sovereignty), and in Asia the ASEAN grouping (built on regional cooperation and the 'ASEAN Way') and, above all, the rise of China (whose reform-driven 'socialist market economy' has made it the world's second-largest economy and a rising global power) — together pointing toward a more multipolar world, in which regional cooperation and economic growth create several centres of influence, and countries like India engage with these centres to advance their interests
There are no changes in the distribution of world power
Regional organisations have no significance
solution: The chapter's overall message is that, as the post-Cold-War UNIPOLAR world evolves, NEW ALTERNATIVE CENTRES of POWER have emerged that can BALANCE and COMPLEMENT US dominance and point toward a more MULTIPOLAR order. The chapter highlights: the EUROPEAN UNION — a deeply INTEGRATED economic and political bloc (built up through decades of integration, formalised by the Maastricht Treaty of 1992, with a common currency, the euro), which commands enormous combined economic clout, trade weight, and diplomatic influence (including UN Security Council seats), though its power to act as one is LIMITED by its members' retained SOVEREIGNTY and differences; and, in ASIA, the ASEAN grouping (founded in 1967, built on regional COOPERATION, the consensual 'ASEAN WAY', and growing economic integration through AFTA and the ASEAN Economic Community), and above all the RISE of CHINA — whose economic REFORMS since 1978 (under Deng Xiaoping), creating a 'SOCIALIST MARKET ECONOMY' (market reforms under continued Communist Party rule), have transformed it into the world's SECOND-LARGEST ECONOMY and a rising military and political power and potential rival/balancer to the USA. Together, these developments — driven by ECONOMIC GROWTH and successful REGIONAL COOPERATION — are creating SEVERAL centres of influence and moving the world toward MULTIPOLARITY. Countries like INDIA respond by ENGAGING with these centres (e.g., through the 'Act East' policy toward ASEAN, economic ties with the EU, and a complex engagement-cum-rivalry with China) to advance their own interests and help shape a multipolar world. So the overall message is option 2.

stem: The EU's origins lie partly in the desire, after two devastating World Wars, to __________.
options: Ensure lasting peace in Europe by binding former enemies (like France and Germany) together through economic cooperation and integration
Rebuild the colonial empires
Prepare for another war
Isolate European countries from each other
solution: The origins of European integration (and eventually the EU) lie partly in the desire, after the two devastating WORLD WARS that had ravaged the continent, to ensure LASTING PEACE in Europe. A central idea was to BIND former ENEMIES — especially FRANCE and GERMANY — so closely TOGETHER through ECONOMIC COOPERATION and INTEGRATION (starting with coal and steel) that another war between them would become unthinkable and practically impossible. Economic interdependence was thus a tool for building durable peace and reconciliation. So the EU's origins lie in securing peace by binding former enemies together. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One reason ASEAN adopted a cautious, consensus-based approach was that __________.
options: Its member states are diverse (in politics, religion, and levels of development) and value their sovereignty, so a non-interfering, consensual approach helped them cooperate despite differences
All its members were identical
It was forced to by the USA
It wanted constant conflict
solution: ASEAN adopted a cautious, consensus-based approach (the 'ASEAN Way') partly because its member states are DIVERSE — differing in political systems, religions, ethnic make-up, and levels of economic DEVELOPMENT — and they strongly VALUE their national SOVEREIGNTY. A NON-INTERFERING (respecting each other's internal affairs), consensual, and non-confrontational approach allowed these varied states to COOPERATE and build trust DESPITE their differences, avoiding the friction that binding rules or interference might cause. So the cautious, consensual approach suited ASEAN's diversity and respect for sovereignty. So option 1 is correct.

stem: ASEAN's regional forums (like the ASEAN Regional Forum) are significant because they __________.
options: Provide a platform for dialogue on political and security issues among ASEAN and other major powers (including the USA, China, and India), promoting regional stability
Are secret military alliances
Exclude all outside powers
Deal only with sports
solution: ASEAN's regional forums — such as the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) — are significant because they provide a PLATFORM for DIALOGUE and consultation on POLITICAL and SECURITY issues, bringing together not only ASEAN members but also OTHER MAJOR POWERS with a stake in the region (including the USA, China, Japan, Russia, and India). By fostering communication, confidence-building, and cooperation among these players, such forums help manage tensions and promote REGIONAL STABILITY and peace. So ASEAN forums enable dialogue among ASEAN and major powers, promoting stability. So option 1 is correct.

stem: China's integration into the world economy was further deepened when it joined the __________ in 2001.
options: World Trade Organisation (WTO)
Warsaw Pact
European Union
NATO
solution: China's integration into the world economy was significantly deepened when it JOINED the WORLD TRADE ORGANISATION (WTO) in 2001. WTO membership gave China greater access to global MARKETS and further integrated it into the rules-based international trading system, accelerating its export-led growth and cementing its role as a major manufacturing and trading power ('the workshop of the world'). So China joined the WTO in 2001. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The economic success of China and other Asian economies has led some to speak of the __________.
options: Shift of economic power/dynamism toward Asia (the 'rise of Asia'/'Asian century')
Decline of all Asian economies
Return of European colonialism
End of all economic growth
solution: The remarkable economic success of CHINA and other dynamic ASIAN economies (like India, and earlier the East Asian 'tigers') has led some to speak of a broad SHIFT of economic power and dynamism TOWARD ASIA — sometimes called the 'RISE of ASIA' or the coming 'ASIAN CENTURY'. This reflects the idea that Asia is becoming an increasingly central and powerful region in the global economy and world affairs, contributing to the emergence of a more multipolar world. So the phenomenon is the shift of economic dynamism toward Asia. So option 1 is correct.

stem: For a country like India, the emergence of multiple power centres is generally advantageous because it __________.
options: Gives India more options and room to manoeuvre — it can build relations with several powers, avoid dependence on any one, and better protect its strategic autonomy and interests
Forces India to pick only one ally forever
Leaves India with no choices
Requires India to give up its independence
solution: For a country like India, the emergence of MULTIPLE power centres (a multipolar world) is generally ADVANTAGEOUS because it gives India more OPTIONS and greater ROOM to MANOEUVRE. India can build and balance relations with SEVERAL major powers (the USA, the EU, Russia, China, Japan, ASEAN, etc.), AVOID excessive DEPENDENCE on any single one, and play them off or partner with different ones as its interests require — thereby better protecting its STRATEGIC AUTONOMY and advancing its national interests. A world of several power centres suits India's traditional preference for independence in foreign policy. So multipolarity gives India more options and protects its autonomy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The EU can influence world affairs through economic diplomacy. Reason (R): Its enormous combined economic and trade power gives it leverage (through market access, aid, and trade agreements) even without a unified military. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the EU can INFLUENCE world affairs through ECONOMIC DIPLOMACY. And the reason is (R) that its ENORMOUS combined economic and TRADE power gives it significant LEVERAGE — through control of access to its vast MARKET, the granting of AID, and the negotiation of TRADE AGREEMENTS and standards — which it can use to influence and shape the behaviour of other countries, EVEN WITHOUT a unified MILITARY force. Its economic weight is thus a primary instrument of its global influence (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The rise of alternative centres of power does NOT necessarily mean the immediate end of US hegemony because __________.
options: The USA still retains enormous advantages (especially military and technological), and the transition to a fully multipolar world is a gradual, ongoing process
The USA has already collapsed
The new centres are all militarily dominant over the USA
Multipolarity has already been fully achieved
solution: The rise of alternative centres of power does NOT necessarily mean the IMMEDIATE END of US hegemony, because the USA still RETAINS ENORMOUS ADVANTAGES — especially its overwhelming MILITARY and TECHNOLOGICAL superiority, its structural economic power, and its soft power — which the emerging centres have not yet matched. Moreover, the shift toward a fully MULTIPOLAR world is a GRADUAL, ONGOING PROCESS: the new centres are still growing and integrating, and each has its own limitations (the EU's internal disunity, ASEAN's modest hard power, China's various challenges). So while power is diffusing, US pre-eminence has not vanished. So option 1 is correct — the transition is gradual and the USA retains major advantages.

stem: The study of alternative centres of power is important for understanding contemporary world politics because it __________.
options: Reveals how the international balance of power is changing, and how regional cooperation and rising economies are reshaping global influence in the 21st century
Concerns only ancient history
Has no bearing on the present
Is only about military alliances
solution: The study of alternative centres of power is important for understanding contemporary world politics because it REVEALS how the international BALANCE of POWER is CHANGING in the 21st century — how REGIONAL COOPERATION (like the EU and ASEAN) and RISING ECONOMIES (like China and India) are RESHAPING global INFLUENCE and moving the world from unipolarity toward multipolarity. Grasping these shifts helps us understand the emerging structure of world politics, the opportunities and challenges it presents, and how countries (including India) position themselves within it. So it illuminates the changing balance of power and the reshaping of global influence. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall relationship of the EU and ASEAN to their members can be summarised as __________.
options: Supranational/regional bodies that enable cooperation and integration while their members remain sovereign states — pooling some functions without abolishing national governments
World governments that have replaced their member states
Military dictatorships ruling the members
Loose clubs with no cooperation at all
solution: The overall relationship of the EU and ASEAN to their members can be summarised thus: they are REGIONAL (and, in the EU's case, partly SUPRANATIONAL) bodies that ENABLE COOPERATION and INTEGRATION among their members — POOLING some functions and decision-making (economic, and in the EU's case also some political/legal matters) — while the members REMAIN SOVEREIGN STATES with their own governments. These organisations do NOT abolish or replace national governments; rather, they provide frameworks through which sovereign states voluntarily cooperate and integrate to varying degrees (the EU more deeply, ASEAN more loosely). So they are cooperation/integration bodies whose members remain sovereign. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter (restated) is that the emergence of alternative centres of power reflects __________.
options: A structural shift in world politics toward a more balanced, multipolar order, driven mainly by economic growth and regional integration rather than by military conquest
A return to European colonial empires
The triumph of a single global government
The complete irrelevance of economics to power
solution: Restated, the overall message is that the emergence of alternative centres of power reflects a STRUCTURAL SHIFT in world politics toward a more BALANCED, MULTIPOLAR order. Crucially, this shift is being driven MAINLY by ECONOMIC GROWTH (the rise of economies like China and India) and by successful REGIONAL INTEGRATION and cooperation (as in the EU and ASEAN) — that is, by economic and institutional means — RATHER than by MILITARY CONQUEST or war. Economic dynamism and cooperative integration, not force, are building the new poles of global influence. So the shift toward multipolarity is driven by economic growth and regional integration. So option 1 is correct.
